topic: model compression; visual prompting; transfer learning; few-shot adaptation
status: bounded synthesis of one sampled full-text benchmark across eight image datasets and a model/method grid
claim: The transfer penalty of a compressed checkpoint is conditional on the adaptation interface, compression procedure and target-data budget; upstream accuracy or parameter count alone does not predict downstream transfer quality. The evidence is specifically about tested vision checkpoints and prompting/transfer protocols, not a universal compression law.
positive_evidence: Misra et al. compare dense and sparse/quantized checkpoints across eight target datasets, multiple ResNet/CLIP/ViT families, and three visual-prompting modes, reporting more than 15,000 experiments.

For compressed CLIP under ILM-VP, 4x compression loses about 45 percentage points on OxfordPets and 24 points on Caltech101, while GTSRB/EuroSAT gaps are around 0-2 points; sparse transfer is particularly fragile at very small target-data budgets.
In cross-modal reprogramming, some 4-bit DeiT results remain near full precision while 2-bit and dataset-specific settings degrade, so the same compression label does not imply a fixed transfer cost.
counterevidence: Dense checkpoints usually outperform compressed checkpoints in the sampled visual-prompting experiments; the finding is not evidence that compression improves transfer overall.
The transfer gaps are small on some datasets and some quantization/budget settings, showing the large OxfordPets example is not representative of every task.
The audit does not compare real deployment latency, energy, current generative LLMs, or all common adaptation pipelines.

sources.sections: Secs. 3.1-3.2; Table 2; quantization and cross-modal reprogramming; supplementary data-budget analyses

falsifiable_test: On post-cutoff vision datasets, compare dense, pruned and quantized checkpoints from matched backbones under visual prompting, linear probe and fine-tuning at 1/2/5/full-shot budgets. Preregister accuracy, calibration, inference latency and energy. The interaction claim weakens if compression method × adaptation × target-data interactions disappear on held-out datasets and upstream accuracy predicts downstream outcomes equally well.
limitations: One sampled benchmark, selected image datasets/checkpoints and visual prompting; three seeds are reported. Result magnitudes must not be generalized to other architectures or adaptation pipelines, and no deployment-level energy/latency experiment was audited.

topic: model compression; subgroup robustness; fairness evaluation
status: bounded synthesis of one sampled EMNLP study and one targeted EMNLP full-text counterexample
claim: Compression does not impose a consistent monotonic penalty on worst-group accuracy or measured social-bias scores. Outcomes vary by dataset, subgroup metric, compression method and model; model size by itself is not an adequate fairness/robustness proxy.
positive_evidence: Gee et al. test 18 compression methods/settings on MultiNLI, CivilComments and SCOTUS: shrinking BERT often lowers worst-group accuracy on MultiNLI/SCOTUS, while many compressed models improve CivilComments worst-group accuracy despite a slight average-accuracy decline.
Within the same study, post-training quantization is generally less subgroup-robust than quantization-aware training, and models at similar parameter counts differ by method/initialization.

Gonçalves and Strubell report dynamic int8 quantization/distillation reducing several measured gender/race/religion bias scores in BERT, RoBERTa and Pythia, consistent with compression sometimes acting as a regularizer on these particular benchmarks.
counterevidence: Compression does worsen worst-group accuracy in many MultiNLI/SCOTUS settings; the claim is conditionality, not guaranteed fairness improvement.

The social-bias study reports category/model-dependent effects and explicitly limits its evidence to three identity dimensions, largely Western bias benchmarks; it says results are preliminary and not production-ready.
The subgroup study is limited to English, BERT variants and three datasets, and evaluates compression procedures largely in isolation.

sources.sections: Methods; subgroup definitions; Sec. 4 results by dataset/method; limitations
Secs. 2-4: BiasBench/model setup, quantization and distillation results, limitations

falsifiable_test: Evaluate dense, quantized, distilled, pruned and quantization-aware models on preregistered multilingual tasks with new label×attribute groups, matching mean accuracy and deployment size where possible. Report subgroup counts, worst-group and average accuracy, calibration and uncertainty. The conditionality claim weakens if worst-group changes are consistently monotonic with size across methods, groups and datasets.
limitations: Two full-text studies with different model families, tasks and fairness definitions; scores are not directly comparable. Neither estimates population-wide fairness effects, and no combined compression methods or production outcomes were tested.

topic: model compression; calibration; uncertainty; sparse and quantized models
status: bounded metric-specific result from one sampled multi-architecture visual-prompting study
claim: In the sampled visual-prompting experiments, pruning/sparsity and quantization show different calibration behavior: increasing sparsity generally worsens ECE, whereas quantization tends to maintain or reduce ECE even when accuracy declines. Therefore, accuracy loss does not determine the direction of calibration change, and compression metrics should be reported separately.
positive_evidence: Misra et al. evaluate ECE and confidence distributions across sparse ResNet/LTH checkpoints and 2-4-bit DeiT/Swin checkpoints, alongside downstream accuracy.

Their sparse-model analysis reports worsening ECE with greater sparsity; quantized models show ECE that is maintained or reduced as precision falls, while confidence on correct/incorrect predictions also shifts.
counterevidence: Quantization is not accuracy-neutral: 2-bit settings can substantially reduce task accuracy, so a calibration improvement would not imply overall model quality improvement.
The direction is reported within particular visual-prompted vision models and ECE/proxy analyses; calibration on other tasks, prevalence shifts or modern LLM outputs was not established.

sources.sections: Sec. 3.2; Figs. 7-13: ECE and confidence analysis; conclusion

falsifiable_test: For matched sparse and quantized checkpoints, evaluate reliability diagrams, ECE, Brier score, selective risk and subgroup calibration under in-domain and shifted visual-prompting/fine-tuning conditions, paired with accuracy and latency. The metric-divergence claim weakens if pruning and quantization calibration changes track accuracy monotonically across held-out tasks and shifts.
limitations: Evidence comes from one paper's vision checkpoints, selected downstream datasets and ECE/confidence summaries. No external replication or deployment-level calibration study was performed.

topic: graph foundation models; self-supervised learning; early stopping; cross-task generalization
status: bounded synthesis of one sampled six-dataset benchmark with explicit counterevidence on small graphs
claim: For the audited graph self-supervised methods, early-stopping/checkpoint selection can favor the downstream task used for validation, but the best choice does not uniformly improve all downstream tasks across graph sizes and training strategies. A single task-specific score is therefore not demonstrated as a reliable universal proxy for graph-transfer quality.
positive_evidence: GraphFM compares eight self-supervised graph methods, six conventional node-feature graphs and node classification/link prediction/clustering; selecting by link prediction can significantly improve that target outcome for contrastive models, while effects on other tasks differ.
On larger graphs, method rankings and outcomes vary by task and node-vs-subgraph mini-batch strategy; runtime-driven Reddit omissions leave the broadest-scale comparison incomplete.
The authors explicitly conclude that no single stopping criterion in their evaluated setup improves all downstream tasks.
counterevidence: On small citation graphs, many node-classification-selected checkpoints also perform well on link prediction and clustering, so cross-task transfer is not uniformly poor.
The benchmark uses a common hyperparameter search budget and reports five-seed full-batch results; the non-universal conclusion is not simply an absence of standardized controls.
falsifiable_test: On held-out graph families and sizes, choose checkpoints with node classification, link prediction, clustering, fixed multi-objective validation, and an unsupervised criterion, then evaluate every choice on every task under fixed compute and tuning budgets. The claim weakens if one selection rule consistently Pareto-dominates across graph families, sizes and task types.
limitations: One benchmark with eight GSSL methods, six numeric-node-feature graphs, selected downstream metrics, and limited Reddit experiments because of runtime. Text-attributed, heterogeneous, temporal and real application graphs are outside the reviewed evidence.
